_comment: USER-FACING release notes, shown in the app: a 'What's new' panel on the dashboard the first
time someone signs in after the running version changes, and the full list under Settings -> About.
THIS IS NOT CHANGELOG.md, AND IT MUST NOT BECOME IT. The changelog is written for whoever
touches the code next and is full of issue numbers, SQL and event-loop arguments. This file is
read by an operator who just wants to know whether anything they do changed. Three to five
bullets, plain language, no issue numbers, no internals, no marketing.
Every released version needs an entry: test/release-notes.test.js fails the build if the
version in VERSION has none, which is what stops this file quietly rotting. Newest first.
'date' is the release date in YYYY-MM-DD.

notes: You can now watch live, sub-second video of what a screen is playing, next to the screenshot you already had. It needs the optional go2rtc sidecar and is off at every level until you turn it on, so nothing starts streaming by itself.

Talk to a screen. Operators can open a voice intercom to one screen or broadcast a PA announcement to many. Off by default, switched on per organization, and an organization can bring its own TURN and STUN servers.

Free trials now end when they are supposed to. A nightly check moves lapsed trials to the Free plan, and you get an email three days before the trial ends and another when it does, saying which screens will stop and how to keep them.
A screen that had been blocked by the plan limit could be quietly switched back on just by assigning it content from the dashboard. It cannot any more.
Screens stopped by an expired trial now say the trial expired, not that a device limit was hit, so it is clear what to do.

You can now require approval before anything goes live. An admin turns it on, picks who reviews, and changes are then submitted, reviewed and published. It is off unless you switch it on, and switching it on leaves everything already playing alone. Nobody can approve their own work.

Everything you edit now keeps a history. Content, playlists, layouts, slide decks and widgets all record who changed what and when, and you can look at an older version, compare it with the current one and restore it. Restoring makes a new draft, so nothing on screen changes until you publish it.

Signs can pull in live information from outside. Point a workspace at a calendar feed and a widget or slide can show whether a room is free, what is booked next and when it frees up. Built by René Gern.
E-paper and microcontroller screens can now show a full multi-zone layout, not just one item, and no longer show unpublished changes before you press Publish. Built by René Gern.

Samsung panels running the 2.0 app showed a black screen. That is fixed, and it needs the panel to be reinstalled with the new build. Screens on some Android TV boxes could also freeze part way through a playlist when screens were synced together, which is fixed too.
Screen background colour works again, LG webOS panels are now supported, and Android displays that were reinstalling the same update over and over will stop.

Fixes a bug in 2.0.6 that left the dashboard blank and showing "Disconnected". Your screens were never affected — they kept playing normally throughout — but the dashboard itself would not load. Please update.
The dashboard no longer makes pointless background requests for the multi-server features on installs that do not use them, which were showing up as errors in the browser console.

E-paper and microcontroller screens are now supported. The server can render what a screen should show as a device-ready image, so a cheap battery panel with no browser on it can be a display. It sleeps between updates and only wakes when something has actually changed.
You can upload your own transition effect. Add a shader file in the transition settings and it appears alongside the built-in effects, on your screens only. The built-in set is unchanged.
The Android app now installs on Android 6.0, so older boxes and tablets can run the full player instead of only a browser page.
Schedules can repeat on specific days of the week, and a repeat can now be given an end date. Both were possible behind the scenes but there was no way to ask for them.
Screens can have their own background colour instead of always black, the weather widget now scales properly in small areas, and the clock can hide its seconds and show dates in your own language.

Transitions on portrait screens are fixed. Every effect was being drawn in landscape shape over a portrait picture, so the image jumped larger at the start of each transition and back at the end. Thanks to Emanuel Mairoll for finding and fixing it.
A clock widget now tells you if the time zone you typed is not a real one, instead of quietly showing UTC or drawing nothing at all. The field also offers a proper list to pick from.
Squares in the layout editor can be dragged properly again. They were only moving to their new position after you clicked a second time.
You can upload far more photos at once, and add many of them to a playlist in one go instead of one at a time. Playlists can also be sorted by name, date or length in a single action.
Self-hosted servers will now correctly see that a newer version is available. The update check could only see older releases, so it kept reporting an out-of-date version as the latest one.

Screens that were refused by the server now come back on their own. A display could get stuck showing “Waiting for content” with everything already downloaded, and only start again if you changed its playlist by hand. That is fixed, on every kind of screen.
Upgrading a busy server no longer leaves browser and Samsung screens stuck on a maintenance message until somebody power-cycles them.
Large installs should feel noticeably lighter. A repair job that ran every time any screen changed item now runs once when a screen reconnects, which is the only time it can find anything to repair.

An Android screen with a full offline cache will now play it after an update, instead of waiting for content it already had. Screens also keep their offline copy when the server sends an empty playlist, so a reboot no longer leaves them with nothing.
Platform admins get a new Diagnostics panel: how the server has been performing day by day, how big the installation is, and a one-click CPU profile to send to support. No shell access needed.

Tightens who can read a display’s web player key. It was already hidden from the display list, and is now also withheld from API tokens — so an integration with read access cannot pick up a key that would let it act as that screen. Your own dashboard still shows it.
Fixes the What’s New panel, which was blank after upgrading to 2.0.1. The notes it reads were missing from the packaged install, so there was nothing to show. Nothing else changed.

Slides can talk. A slide can carry a voiceover and a deck can carry background music that plays underneath the whole thing, on every kind of screen — and audio files can now be uploaded, which the content library used to refuse. Screens stay silent unless you ask for sound.

Slides keep the shape you designed them in. A deck laid out as widescreen no longer stretches to fit a taller or wider screen, which used to crop the background and push headlines off the edge. It is centred at its own shape instead, and text on older Android screens is finally the size you set.

Setup now leaves a screen actually playing. The last step asks what the display should play and offers the playlists you already have, and content uploaded during setup is published rather than left as a draft on a blank screen. The checklist follows you through it.

A first start no longer gets overwhelmed by its own screens. On large installs the server finishes its upgrade work before letting displays reconnect, and says what it is doing while it works — so a slow disk looks slow rather than broken.

Displays can be given a web player URL, for players that lose their storage when they restart — a browser input in vMix, for instance, which used to come back as a brand new display every time it was reopened. It is off unless you ask for it.
Slides: a proper editor for text, numbers, photos, clocks and QR codes, where the wording and the layout are separate — so changing a headline months later does not disturb the design.
Triggers: a screen can switch to different content on a signal, and switch back afterwards.
Playlists can contain other playlists, and a screen can inherit its playlist from its group or video wall.
Multi-site: link separate servers so one dashboard can see screens at other locations.
Play reporting survives an outage — a player records what it showed while offline and sends it once it reconnects.
Workspaces and single sign-on, for teams that need separate spaces or a company login.
